claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading is dominated by interfacial diffusion creep.
Stress-induced changes in local chemical short-range order activate the proposed diffusion-creep mechanism.
Dislocation nucleation is enhanced at nanoscale interfaces under sustained loading.
The starting coating consists of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with coherent interfaces.
The starting interfaces have homogeneous short-range order.
Changing loading rate can expose both dislocation-mediated and diffusion-dominated creep behavior.
Nanoscale interfaces and their local atomic short-range order govern the deformation response.
Applied load induces local variations in chemical short-range order at the interfaces.
Interfacial short-range-order variations lower the activation barrier for dislocation nucleation.
The creep mechanism can transition from dislocation-driven creep to diffusion creep as loading rate changes.
The diffusion-creep regime proceeds by direct atom-vacancy exchange.
The transition to diffusion creep produces smoother and more homogeneous plastic flow across the multilayer.
Higher loading rates will produce a lower creep stress exponent than the lower-rate baseline.
Higher loading rates will increase atomic diffusion at the multilayer interfaces.
Sustained loading will produce microscopically observable changes in interfacial short-range order.
At lower loading rates, the baseline response has a higher creep stress exponent.
At lower loading rates, dislocations form distinct pile-ups at the multilayer interfaces.
Catastrophic shear banding or interfacial decohesion would override the proposed creep mechanism.
Failure to observe a stress-exponent reduction, stress-induced short-range-order changes, and enhanced interfacial diffusion relative to baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The top-level hypothesis broadly says deformation under sustained loading is dominated by diffusion creep, whereas the conditions, mechanism, and baseline describe a rate-dependent regime in which lower-rate deformation is primarily dislocation-mediated.
